groups.title: Alex's Training
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

transcript.text: Hi Alex.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: It’s Martha Clines here.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: James White gave me your number.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I hope you don’t mind me calling you.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Of course not.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: How are you, Martha?
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Good thanks.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I’m ringing because I need a bit of advice.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Oh yeah.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: What about?
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: The training you did at JPNW a few years ago.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I’m applying for the same thing.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Oh right.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Yes, I did mine in 2014.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Best thing I ever did.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I’m still working there.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Really?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: What are you doing?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Well, now I work in the customer services department but I did my initial training in Finance.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I stayed there for the first two years and then moved to where I am now.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: That’s the same department I’m applying for.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Did you enjoy it?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I was pretty nervous to begin with.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I didn’t do well in my exams at school and I was really worried because I failed Maths.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: But it didn’t actually matter because I did lots of courses on the job.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Did you get a diploma at the end of your trainee period?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I’m hoping to do the one in business skills.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: That sounds good.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I took the one on IT skills but I wish I’d done that one instead.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: OK, that’s good to know.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: What about the other trainees?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: How did you get on with them?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: There were about 20 of us who started at the same time and we were all around the same age – I was 18 and there was only one person younger than me, who was 17.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: The rest were between 18 and 20.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I made some good friends.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I’ve heard lots of good things about the training at JPNW.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: It seems like there are a lot of opportunities there.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Yeah, definitely.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Because of its size you can work in loads of different areas within the organisation.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: What about pay?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: I know you get a lower minimum wage than regular employees.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: That’s right – which isn’t great.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: But you get the same number of days’ holiday as everyone else.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: And the pay goes up massively if they offer you a job at the end of the training period.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Yeah, but I’m not doing it for the money – it’s the experience I think will be really useful.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Everyone says by the end of the year you gain so much confidence.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: You’re right.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: That’s the most useful part about it.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: There’s a lot of variety too.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: You’re given lots of different things to do.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I enjoyed it all – I didn’t even mind the studying.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Do you have to spend any time in college?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Yes, one day each month.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: So you get lots of support from both your tutor and your manager.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: That’s good.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: And the company is easy to get to, isn’t it?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Yes, it’s very close to the train station so the location’s a real advantage.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Have you got a date for your interview yet?
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Yes, it’s on the 23rd of this month.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: So long as you’re well prepared there’s nothing to worry about.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Everyone’s very friendly.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I am not sure what I should wear.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: What do you think?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Nothing too casual – like jeans, for example.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: If you’ve got a nice jacket, wear that with a skirt or trousers.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Thanks.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Any other tips?
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Erm, well I know it’s really obvious but arrive in plenty of time.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: They hate people who are late.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: So make sure you know exactly where you have to get to.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: And one other useful piece of advice my manager told me before I had the interview for this job – is to smile.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Even if you feel terrified.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: It makes people respond better to you.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: I’ll have to practise doing that in the mirror!
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Yeah – well, good luck.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Let me know if you need any more information.
transcript.speaker: ALEX

transcript.text: Thanks very much.
transcript.speaker: MARTHA

transcript.text: Hi everyone, welcome to the Snow Centre.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: My name’s Annie.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I hope you enjoyed the bus trip from the airport – we’ve certainly got plenty of snow today!
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Well, you’ve come to New Zealand’s premier snow and ski centre, and we’ve a whole load of activities for you during your week here.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Most visitors come here for the cross-country skiing, where you’re on fairly flat ground for most of the time, rather than going down steep mountainsides.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There are marked trails, but you can also leave these and go off on your own and that’s an experience not to be missed.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You can go at your own speed – it’s great aerobic exercise if you really push yourself, or if you prefer you can just glide gently along and enjoy the beautiful scenery.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This afternoon, you’ll be going on a dog-sled trip.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You may have seen our dogs on TV recently racing in the winter sled festival.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you want, you can have your own team for the afternoon and learn how to drive them, following behind our leader on the trail.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Or if you’d prefer, you can just sit back in the sled and enjoy the ride as a passenger.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: At the weekend, we have the team relay event, and you’re all welcome to join in.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We have a local school coming along, and a lot of the teachers are taking part too.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Participation rather than winning is the main focus, and there’s a medal for everyone who takes part.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Participants are in teams of two to four, and each team must complete four laps of the course.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: For your final expedition, you’ll head off to Mount Frenner wearing a pair of special snow shoes which allow you to walk on top of the snow.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This is an area where miners once searched for gold, though there are very few traces of their work left now.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: When the snow melts in summer, the mountain slopes are carpeted in flowers and plants.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s a long ascent, though not too steep, and walkers generally take a couple of days to get to the summit and return.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You’ll spend the night in our hut half-way up the mountain.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s included in your package for the stay.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s got cooking facilities, firewood and water for drinking.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: For washing, we recommend you use melted snow, though, to conserve supplies.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We can take your luggage up on our snowmobile for you for just ten dollars a person.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The hut has cooking facilities so you can make a hot meal in the evening and morning, but you need to take your own food.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The weather on Mount Frenner can be very stormy.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In that case, stay in the hut – generally the storms don’t last long.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Don’t stress about getting back here to the centre in time to catch the airport bus – they’ll probably not be running anyway.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We do have an emergency locator beacon in the hut but only use that if it’s real emergency, like if someone’s ill or injured.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, let me tell you something about the different ski trails you can follow during your stay here.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Highland Trail’s directly accessible from where we are now.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This trail’s been designed to give first-timers an experience they’ll enjoy regardless of their age or skill, but it’s also ideal for experts to practise their technique.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Then there’s Pine Trail … if you’re nervous about skiing, leave this one to the experts!
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You follow a steep valley looking right down on the river below – scary!
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: But if you’ve fully mastered the techniques needed for hills, it’s great fun.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Stony Trail’s a good choice once you’ve got a general idea of the basics.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There are one or two tricky sections, but nothing too challenging.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’s a shelter half-way where you can sit and take a break and enjoy the afternoon sunshine.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And finally, Loser’s Trail.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This starts off following a gentle river valley but the last part is quite exposed so the snow conditions can be challenging – if it’s snowing or windy, check with us before you set out to make sure the trail’s open that day.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Right, so now if you’d like to follow me, we’ll get started …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’ve still got loads to do for our report on nutritional food labels.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Me too.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: What did you learn from doing the project about your own shopping habits?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Well, I’ve always had to check labels for traces of peanuts in everything I eat because of my allergy.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: But beyond that I’ve never really been concerned enough to check how healthy a product is.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: This project has actually taught me to read the labels much more carefully.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I tended to believe claims on packaging like ‘low in fat’.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But I now realise that the ‘healthy’ yoghurt I’ve bought for years is full of sugar and that it’s actually quite high in calories.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Ready meals are the worst … comparing the labels on supermarket pizzas was a real eye-opener.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Did you have any idea how many calories they contain?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I was amazed.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Yes, because unless you read the label really carefully, you wouldn’t know that the nutritional values given are for half a pizza.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: When most people eat the whole pizza.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Not exactly transparent is it?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Not at all.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But I expect it won’t stop you from buying pizza?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Probably not, no!
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I thought comparing the different labelling systems used by food manufacturers was interesting.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think the kind of labelling system used makes a big difference.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Which one did you prefer?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I liked the traditional daily value system best – the one which tells you what proportion of your required daily intake of each ingredient the product contains.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I’m not sure it’s the easiest for people to use but at least you get the full story.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I like to know all the ingredients in a product – not just how much fat, salt and sugar they contain.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: But it’s good supermarkets have been making an effort to provide reliable information for customers.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: There just needs to be more consistency between labelling systems used by different supermarkets, in terms of portion sizes, etc.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: The labels on the different brands of chicken flavour crisps were quite revealing too, weren’t they?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I don’t understand how they can get away with calling them chicken flavour when they only contain artificial additives.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I know.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I’d at least have expected them to contain a small percentage of real chicken.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Absolutely.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think having nutritional food labeling has been a good idea, don’t you?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I think it will change people’s behaviour and stop mothers, in particular, buying the wrong things.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But didn’t that study kind of prove the opposite?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: People didn’t necessarily stop buying unhealthy products.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: They only said that might be the case.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Those findings weren’t that conclusive and it was quite a small-scale study.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I think more research has to be done.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Yes, I think you’re probably right.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: What do you think of the traffic-light system?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think supermarkets like the idea of having a colour-coded system – red, orange or green – for levels of fat, sugar and salt in a product.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But it’s not been adopted universally.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: And not on all products.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Why do you suppose that is?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Pressure from the food manufacturers.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Hardly surprising that some of them are opposed to flagging up how unhealthy their products are.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I’d have thought it would have been compulsory. It seems ridiculous it isn’t.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I know.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: And what I couldn’t get over is the fact that it was brought in without enough consultation – a lot of experts had deep reservations about it.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: That is a bit weird.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I suppose there’s an argument for doing the research now when consumers are familiar with this system.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Yeah, maybe.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: The participants in the survey were quite positive about the traffic-light system.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Mmm.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But I don’t think they targeted the right people.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: They should have focused on people with low literacy levels because these labels are designed to be accessible to them.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: But it’s good to get feedback from all socio-economic groups.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: And there wasn’t much variation in their responses.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: But if they hadn’t interviewed participants face-to-face, they could have used a much bigger sample size.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: I wonder why they chose that method?
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: Dunno.
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: How were they selected?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: Did they volunteer or were they approached?
transcript.speaker: JACK

transcript.text: I think they volunteered.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

transcript.text: The thing that wasn’t stated was how often they bought packaged food – all we know is how frequently they used the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: ALICE

groups.title: The history of coffee
groups.instruction: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

transcript.text: In my presentation, I’m going to talk about coffee, and its importance both in economic and social terms.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: We think it was first drunk in the Arab world, but there’s hardly any documentary evidence of it before the 1500s, although of course that doesn’t mean that people didn’t know about it before then.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, there is evidence that coffee was originally gathered from bushes growing wild in Ethiopia, in the northeast of Africa.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the early sixteenth century, it was being bought by traders, and gradually its use as a drink spread throughout the Middle East.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s also known that in 1522, in the Turkish city of Constantinople, which was the centre of the Ottoman Empire, the court physician approved its use as a medicine.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: By the mid-1500s, coffee bushes were being cultivated in the Yemen and for the next hundred years this region produced most of the coffee drunk in Africa and the Arab world.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: What’s particularly interesting about coffee is its effect on social life.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It was rarely drunk at home, but instead people went to coffee houses to drink it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These people, usually men, would meet to drink coffee and chat about issues of the day.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But at the time, this chance to share ideas and opinions was seen as something that was potentially dangerous, and in 1623 the ruler of Constantinople demanded the destruction of all the coffee houses in the city, although after his death many new ones opened, and coffee consumption continued.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the seventeenth century, coffee drinking spread to Europe, and here too coffee shops became places where ordinary people, nearly always men, could meet to exchange ideas.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Because of this, some people said that these places performed a similar function to universities.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The opportunity they provided for people to meet together outside their own homes and to discuss the topics of the day had an enormous impact on social life, and many social movements and political developments had their origins in coffee house discussions.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the late 1600s, the Yemeni monopoly on coffee production broke down and coffee production started to spread around the world, helped by European colonization.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Europeans set up coffee plantations in Indonesia and the Caribbean and production of coffee in the colonies skyrocketed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Different types of coffee were produced in different areas, and it’s interesting that the names given to these different types, like Mocha or Java coffee, were often taken from the port they were shipped to Europe from.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But if you look at the labour system in the different colonies, there were some significant differences.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In Brazil and the various Caribbean colonies, coffee was grown in huge plantations and the workers there were almost all slaves.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But this wasn’t the same in all colonies; for example in Java, which had been colonized by the Dutch, the peasants grew coffee and passed a proportion of this on to the Dutch, so it was used as a means of taxation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But whatever system was used, under the European powers of the eighteenth century, coffee production was very closely linked to colonisation.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Coffee was grown in ever-increasing quantities to satisfy the growing demand from Europe, and it became nearly as important as sugar production, which was grown under very similar conditions.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, coffee prices were not yet low enough for people to drink it regularly at home, so most coffee consumption still took place in public coffee houses and it still remained something of a luxury item.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In Britain, however, a new drink was introduced from China, and started to become popular, gradually taking over from coffee, although at first it was so expensive that only the upper classes could afford it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This was tea, and by the late 1700s it was being widely drunk.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: However, when the USA gained independence from Britain in 1766, they identified this drink with Britain, and coffee remained the preferred drink in the USA, as it still is today.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, by the early nineteenth century, coffee was already being widely produced and consumed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But during this century, production boomed and coffee prices started to fall.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This was partly because new types of transportation had been developed which were cheaper and more efficient.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So now, working people could afford to buy coffee – it wasn’t just a drink for the middle classes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And this was at a time when large parts of Europe were starting to work in industries.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: And sometimes this meant their work didn’t stop when it got dark; they might have to continue throughout the night.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So, the use of coffee as a stimulant became important – it wasn’t just a drink people drank in the morning, for breakfast.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There were also changes in cultivation …
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
